track.name: ux
track.label: UX & Discovery
track.summary: Go from a blank whiteboard to a tested prototype — the user research, design and communication skills every product team assumes you already have.

phases.title: Foundations of UX & Human-Centered Design
phases.description: What UX design actually is, how design thinking structures the work, and where it sits relative to UI and product design.

phases.title: User Research Methods
phases.description: Talk to real users, run surveys that produce useful data, and turn what you learn into personas and journey maps.

phases.title: Information Architecture & Interaction Design
phases.description: Structure content so people can find it, and apply the interaction principles that make an interface feel obvious.

phases.title: Wireframing & Prototyping
phases.description: Sketch the bones of a screen, then build a clickable prototype and reusable components in Figma.

phases.title: Usability Testing & Iteration
phases.description: Watch real people use your design, evaluate it against known heuristics, and iterate with A/B tests.

phases.title: UX Strategy & Stakeholder Communication
phases.description: Present design decisions persuasively, prove their value with metrics, and design for every user including people with disabilities.

topics.title: What is UX Design?
topics.description: A working definition of UX design and why it's become central to how digital products get built.

steps.t: Define UX design in your words
steps.d: Write a clear definition of UX design that distinguishes it from UI design, product design, and graphic design using examples from a real product.

steps.t: Map the scope of UX work
steps.d: List the activities UX designers actually do (research, wireframing, prototyping, testing, etc.) and identify which activities have nothing to do with how things look.
Use a product you find difficult, document three moments where you were confused or had to guess, then describe what information or flow change would have helped.

steps.t: Identify UX decisions in an app
steps.d: Open an app you use daily and name three UX decisions (not visual design, but interaction design) that affect how easily you get something done.

steps.t: Justify UX investment to a skeptic
steps.d: Explain to a non-designer why spending a week on UX research and testing is worth more than shipping features faster.

topics.title: The Design Thinking Process
topics.description: The empathize-define-ideate-prototype-test cycle that structures most human-centered design work.

steps.d: Take a product you know well and trace how the design thinking cycle (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test) would actually play out over one quarter.
Spend an hour watching someone else use a product you know, writing down every place they hesitate, backtrack, or seem confused.
Take what you observed and write one clear problem statement that captures what someone is trying to do but can't.
Sketch three completely different approaches to solving the problem you defined, not iterations on one idea.
Build or sketch a prototype of the most promising idea and show it to someone (not the designer) to see whether it actually solves the problem you identified.

topics.title: UX vs UI vs Product Design
topics.description: How these three commonly confused roles actually divide up the work of building a product.

steps.d: Take a screen and describe three UX decisions (information hierarchy, interaction flow, terminology) and three UI decisions (color, typeface, spacing) and explain why they're different.
List what a UX designer, UI designer, and product designer each own in a product team, and name one decision that might involve all three roles.
Take a feature that launched recently and identify whether the workflow (what steps a user takes) was decided by UX, UI, or product, based on the artifacts and process.
Talk to your UX and UI designers (if you have them) and document where they disagree about who should decide a design choice.
Write a one-page guide for your team clarifying whether UX, UI, or product owns interaction flow, visual hierarchy, and color system.

topics.title: Recruiting and Screening Participants
topics.description: Who you test with decides what you learn — sourcing, screening and incentives before any session is booked.

steps.t: Define the participant in one line
steps.d: The behaviour that qualifies someone, not the demographic. "Has booked travel on a phone in the last month" beats "25-40, urban".
Include one question whose wrong answer disqualifies, and avoid any question that tells them which answer you want.

steps.t: Pick the channel and the incentive
steps.d: Decide where you will post and what you will offer. An unpaid ask recruits the unusually keen, which is its own bias.
Test the script on a colleague first. You will cut two questions and reorder two more.

steps.t: Record who you could not get
steps.d: Note the group that did not respond, and carry that limitation into how you report the results.

topics.title: User Interviews
topics.description: Plan and run one-on-one conversations that surface real user needs instead of assumptions.

steps.d: Prepare five to seven open-ended questions that would help you discover how someone actually uses the product you are researching and what frustrates them.
Find and recruit three users who match your target audience and schedule 45-minute interviews with each over the next two weeks.
Run at least one user interview, with permission record it or take detailed notes, and write down at least three moments where the user did something unexpected.
Compare notes across your three interviews and write down the three most common frustrations you heard, counting how many people mentioned each.
Compare what you heard to what you believed before the interviews and list at least one assumption that the interviews proved wrong.

topics.title: Surveys & Quantitative Research
topics.description: Write survey questions that produce clean, analyzable data instead of noise.

steps.d: Draft ten questions about how people use a specific product (not yes-or-no questions, but scaled or open-ended) that would produce analyzable data.
Ask five people to review your questions aloud and tell you what they mean — revise any question that people interpret differently.
Decide how many responses you need to get a reliable answer to your research question, then calculate how long it'll take to recruit that many people.
Send out your survey and collect at least 50 responses, then create a spreadsheet showing the distribution of answers to each question.
Take the three most common frustrations you found in user interviews and look for them in your survey data — did you find confirmation or contradiction.

topics.title: Personas & Journey Mapping
topics.description: Turn research findings into personas and journey maps the whole team can design against.

steps.d: Review all your interview and survey notes and write down the three to five distinct user archetypes (different goals, workflows, or frustrations) that emerged.
Pick one archetype and create a one-page persona with a name, actual goals (from interviews, not guesses), and three key behaviors you observed.

steps.t: Map a journey for that persona
steps.d: Trace the workflow of your persona trying to accomplish their main goal in your product, including every step, feeling, and potential stumble point.

steps.t: Test the personas with your team
steps.d: Show your personas and journey map to your product and engineering leads and ask whether they recognize these users from their own customer conversations.

steps.t: Use them to guide a decision
steps.d: Take one feature you're about to build and use your personas and journey maps to argue for one design direction over another.

topics.title: Information Architecture Fundamentals
topics.description: Organize content into structures people can actually navigate.

steps.d: List every type of content, page, or section in your product (e.g., posts, comments, user profiles, settings) and group similar items together.
Draw a diagram showing how your content inventory would be organized so users could actually find things (not your company's structure, but their mental model).
Watch three people try to find something on your site using your proposed structure and write down whether they looked in the right place first or had to search.
Compare your proposed information architecture to how your product is actually organized today and identify at least one major difference.
Reorganize one section of your product based on your IA (even in a wireframe or prototype) and measure whether people find things faster.

topics.title: Card Sorting & Sitemaps
topics.description: Use card sorting to discover how users group content, then turn that into a sitemap.

steps.d: Write 20-30 item names (content types, features, or page names) on cards and recruit 8-10 users to sort them however makes sense to them.
Facilitate the card sort sessions (in person or online) and record how each user grouped the items and what they named each group.
Look for consensus — which items consistently end up together, which were controversial, and where users created entirely new categories.
Compare the groupings users made to the information architecture you had in mind and write down at least one group that surprised you.
Use the card sort results to create a sitemap or information architecture showing the main categories and subcategories users would actually expect.

topics.title: Interaction Design Principles
topics.description: The psychology-backed rules — Fitts's Law, Hick's Law, and more — behind interfaces that feel intuitive.

steps.d: Describe Fitts's Law (the farther or smaller a target, the longer it takes to click it) and identify one place in a product you use where it's violated.
Look at a screen with more than ten options and describe using Hick's Law why a user might feel overwhelmed, then propose a change to reduce choices.
Find an interactive element in a product and ask three people whether they can tell it's clickable by looking at it — if not, it lacks affordance.
Walk through a workflow in an app you use and name three places where interaction design made something harder than it should be.
Take one of those violations and sketch a redesign that applies Fitts's, Hick's, or affordance principles to make the interaction more intuitive.

topics.title: Low-Fidelity Wireframing
topics.description: Rough out a screen's layout and flow before investing in visual design.

steps.d: Sketch a wireframe of a single screen on paper or in a tool, showing only layout, hierarchy, and content areas (no colors, no real text).
Make sure your wireframe shows where the user will find navigation, the main content, calls to action, and any secondary elements they might need.
Show your wireframe to three people and ask them to point out the most important thing on the screen and where they'd tap to do the main action.
Redraw your wireframe based on what people got wrong or missed in the test and do a second round of user feedback.
Create wireframes for three to five screens showing the complete user flow (from entry point to completion of a key task).

topics.title: Prototyping with Figma
topics.description: Wire frames together into a clickable prototype someone else can actually test.

steps.d: Take your wireframes and recreate them in Figma with simple shapes and placeholder text.
Use Figma's prototype feature to add click targets on buttons, links, and interactive elements that jump to the next screen.
Hand someone your Figma prototype and ask them to complete a task by clicking through it — observe where they get confused or click the wrong thing.
Based on the test, add or adjust interactions to guide users toward the right action (e.g., button placement, confirmation messages).
Add basic visual design (typography, color, spacing) to your prototype so it feels closer to a real product, not wireframe gray boxes.

topics.title: Design Systems & Component Libraries
topics.description: Reusable components and a shared design system that keep a product consistent as it grows.

steps.d: Look at your product and list every reusable piece (buttons, input fields, cards, modals, etc.) and count how many times each appears across your screens.
In Figma, build the ten most-used components, each with at least two variants (e.g., button in primary, secondary, and disabled states).
Create a one-page guide showing each component, what it's for, when to use it, and what states or variants it has.
Use only your components to redesign one existing screen and compare it to the original — list every place where your redesign looks different.
Have your team use the component library for their next design and document where components felt restrictive or where you needed new ones.

topics.title: Usability Testing Fundamentals
topics.description: Watch real people attempt real tasks to find out where a design actually breaks down.

steps.d: Find and schedule five users who match your target audience for 30-minute usability testing sessions over the next three weeks.
Write a script with three to four realistic tasks (e.g., 'find and add this item to your cart') that someone would actually do in your product.
Run the sessions with permission to record or take detailed notes, observing where each person succeeds, struggles, hesitates, or gives up.
Compare notes across the five tests and identify the one task where the most people got stuck or gave up.
For each failure point, sketch a design change and predict why it would help, testing your prediction with one more user.

topics.title: Heuristic Evaluation
topics.description: Audit an interface against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics without needing to recruit test users.

steps.d: Review through Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics (visibility of system status, match between system and real world, etc.) and write one example of each from a real product.
Apply all ten heuristics to evaluate a product you're redesigning, and write down at least three places where it violates one.
Have two designers who didn't work on the product evaluate it against the heuristics independently and compare notes.
Take the violations you found and rank them by how many users would hit that problem and how much it would block them.
For the top three violations, sketch how you'd redesign that part of the product to align with the heuristic.

topics.title: A/B Testing & Iteration
topics.description: Test one change at a time against real traffic to know whether it actually helped.

steps.d: Write a specific hypothesis about a design change: 'If we move the button here, checkout abandonment will drop by 5%'.
Describe the control version, the variant version, how many visitors you need per group, and how many days the test should run.
Actually run an A/B test with your proposed design change against the current design, collecting at least 500 visitors per group.
Compare the key metric (conversion, completion time, error rate) between control and variant and determine whether the difference is statistically significant.
If the variant won, roll it out; if not, describe why your hypothesis was wrong and what you'd test next.

topics.title: Presenting Design Work
topics.description: Frame design decisions around the story and the business outcome stakeholders actually care about.

steps.d: Before presenting, write down exactly who your stakeholder is, what they care about (money, speed, user retention), and what they'd say 'no' to.
Structure your design presentation around the customer problem and the outcome, spending 30 seconds on why this matters before showing a single screen.
Present at least two design approaches and explicitly state what each gives up so your audience understands why you chose one.
Describe what would prove your design worked (specific measurable outcome, not 'users will like it more') and how you'll know if you shipped the wrong thing.
When someone asks you to change the design, write down their concern as a metric or outcome and explain how your design actually addresses it.

topics.title: UX Metrics & ROI
topics.description: Track the numbers — conversion, retention, support cost — that make the case for design investment.

steps.d: Decide which business metric actually reflects the value of your design — conversion, task completion time, or retention — and explain why not activity.
For your chosen metric, record the current value before your design launches so you have something to compare against.
Define what improvement would justify the design work — a 5% lift, 10% lift, or something else — and write down why that number matters to the business.
After your design ships, track the metric weekly for at least four weeks and compare against your baseline and target.
Translate your metric improvement into business language (time saved, dollars earned, retention gained) and show it to leadership.

topics.title: Accessibility Fundamentals
topics.description: Design and build for people using assistive technology, using WCAG as the baseline.

steps.d: Review the WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria (color contrast, font size, alternative text) and identify one page in your product that violates three of them.
Download a free screen reader and navigate your product using only keyboard and voice — write down what's confusing or broken.

steps.t: Test with an assistive tech user
steps.d: If possible, watch someone who uses assistive technology (screen reader, voice control, switch) try to complete a task in your product.
Take one component that failed accessibility testing and redesign it to meet WCAG Level AA (better contrast, descriptive label, keyboard navigation).
Create a guide for your team on the five most common accessibility issues in your type of product and how to avoid each one.
